title: Ledgers
outcomes: Explain what a ledger is and how it differs from the journal.
Post journal entries — simple and compound — into ledger accounts with the right "To" and "By" wording.
Balance an account and carry the balance down correctly to the next period.
Say which accounts are balanced and carried forward and which are closed by transfer at the year end.

meta.exam_tip: Ledger accounts are usually asked as part of a bigger question. Neat posting and correct balancing earn quick marks.

concepts.title: The ledger: the principal book
body: The journal records transactions in date order. The ledger regroups the same information account by account, so you can see the full story of Cash, Rohan or Rent in one place.
Every account has a page (folio). The folio number is written in the L.F. column of the journal, and the journal page in the J.F. column of the ledger, so you can trace an entry both ways.
concepts.analogy: The journal is your phone's call log in time order; the ledger is the same calls grouped by contact.
concepts.work: When a client asks "how much does this customer owe us?", nobody reads the journal — you open the customer's ledger account. Auditors also send balance confirmations straight from ledger balances.

concepts.title: Posting rules
body: For the account debited in the journal: write on its debit side, "To" + the name of the account credited, with date, J.F. and amount.
For the account credited: write on its credit side, "By" + the name of the account debited.
Compound entry: each account is posted with its own amount. The single account on one side shows each of the other accounts separately (or the word "Sundries" for the total).
concepts.analogy: In each account you write where the money went to or came from — like writing the sender's name on a received parcel.
concepts.work: Software posts automatically, but you still read ledgers to find mistakes. If Rent Account shows "By Sales", something was posted to the wrong side.

concepts.title: Balancing an account
body: Total both sides. Write the difference on the lighter side as "Balance c/d" (carried down), so both totals become equal. Then bring it down on the opposite side as "Balance b/d" (brought down) at the start of the next period.

A debit balance means the debit side was heavier (assets, expenses, debtors). A credit balance means the credit side was heavier (liabilities, capital, incomes, creditors). If both sides are equal, the account is simply closed.
concepts.analogy: Like closing a school notebook at term end: you write the final score, rule off, and start the next page with that score.
concepts.work: A debtor with a credit balance (customer has paid too much) or a cash account with a credit balance (impossible) is an instant warning sign during ledger scrutiny.

concepts.title: Balanced or closed at the year end?
body: Personal and real accounts (debtors, creditors, capital, cash, bank, assets) are balanced and their balances carried forward — they continue into next year.
Nominal accounts (expenses, losses, incomes, gains) are not carried forward. At the year end they are closed by transfer to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account, so next year starts with zero.
concepts.analogy: Your savings carry over to next year; your monthly phone bill does not — each year's bills are counted in that year only.
concepts.work: If a nominal account shows an opening balance on 1 April, the year-end closing entries were missed — a classic finding when you take over a new client's books.

concepts.title: Two common formats
body: T-form (traditional): two sides, Dr and Cr, each with Date, Particulars, J.F. and Amount. This is the exam format.
Running-balance form: one list with Dr, Cr and a Balance column after every entry. This is how accounting software and bank statements show an account.
concepts.analogy: The T-form is a two-team scoreboard; the running-balance form is a live score ticker.
concepts.work: You will read running-balance ledgers every day at work, but write T-form ledgers in the exam unless asked otherwise.

jobs.title: Ledger scrutiny before the audit
jobs.situation: The client's accountant sends the general ledger for the year. Your senior asks you to "scrutinise the ledger" and list anything unusual before fieldwork starts.
steps: Scan each account for balances on the wrong side: debtors with credit balances, creditors with debit balances, cash with a credit balance.
Look for nominal accounts with opening balances — year-end closing entries may be missing.
Pick large or round-sum entries and odd narrations ("adjustment", "as per sir") for vouching.
Agree the ledger balances to the trial balance the client gave you.
jobs.takeaway: Knowing which side each kind of account normally balances on lets you spot errors in minutes.
jobs.think: A customer account shows a credit balance of ₹12,000. Give two possible reasons.
jobs.answer: The customer paid in advance or paid twice, or a receipt was posted to the wrong customer, or a credit note was entered twice. Each needs checking with documents.

jobs.title: Sending balance confirmations
jobs.role: Accounts executive at a distribution company
jobs.situation: At the year end your company asks its top 20 customers and suppliers to confirm the balance they show for you.
steps: Take each party's closing balance from its ledger account.
Send a statement of account (the ledger in running-balance form) and ask them to confirm or report differences.
For each difference, compare entry by entry — usually a payment in transit, a missing invoice or a credit note not yet recorded.
jobs.takeaway: Ledger accounts are not just for exams — they are the documents you share with outsiders.
jobs.think: Your books show the supplier is owed ₹80,000; the supplier says ₹95,000. What is the first thing to look for?
jobs.answer: An invoice of ₹15,000 the supplier has raised but you have not yet recorded (or a payment you recorded that they have not received).

mcqs.q: Cash paid to Arun ₹5,000 is posted in Arun's account as:
options: To Cash A/c on the debit side
By Cash A/c on the credit side
To Arun A/c on the debit side
By Arun A/c on the debit side
mcqs.explain: The journal entry is Arun A/c Dr. To Cash A/c, because Arun receives the cash. In Arun's account the posting goes on the debit side and names the other account in the entry: 'To Cash A/c ₹5,000'. The tempting option, 'By Cash A/c on the credit side', is how the same amount appears in the Cash Account, not in Arun's account. In practice: when a Tally user opens Arun's ledger, the payment appears as a debit showing Cash as the contra account.

mcqs.q: When the debit side of an account is heavier, the account has:
mcqs.explain: An account's balance is named after the heavier side: if debits exceed credits, the account has a debit balance. 'Balance c/d' is written on the lighter (credit) side to make both totals equal. The tempting option, 'a credit balance', confuses the side where Balance c/d is written with the nature of the balance. In practice: a customer's account with a debit balance means the customer still owes the business — it appears among trade receivables.

mcqs.q: Which of these accounts is closed by transfer to the Profit and Loss Account at the year end?
mcqs.explain: Nominal accounts — expenses, losses, incomes and gains — are closed at year end by transfer to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account; Rent Paid is an expense, so it is closed this way. Real and personal accounts such as Machinery, Bank and Capital are balanced and carried forward to the next year. The tempting option, Capital, is credited with the year's profit but is never closed. In practice: closing entries in Tally reset all expense ledgers to zero at the start of each financial year.

mcqs.q: An account shows: debit total ₹84,500, credit total ₹61,200. The balance is:
mcqs.explain: Balance = heavier side − lighter side = ₹84,500 − ₹61,200 = ₹23,300. The debit side is heavier, so the account has a debit balance of ₹23,300; Balance c/d is written on the credit side. The tempting option, ₹23,300 Cr, has the right amount but takes its name from the side where Balance c/d is written. In practice: an accountant reconciling a supplier's statement checks both the amount and whether the balance is debit or credit.

mcqs.q: The "L.F." column in the journal shows:
options: The ledger page where the entry is posted
mcqs.explain: L.F. stands for ledger folio — the page number of the account in the ledger to which the journal entry has been posted. It is filled in at the time of posting, so it shows that posting has been done and helps trace the entry later. The tempting option, the voucher number, is a document reference, not a ledger reference. In practice: auditors use ledger folio references in manual books to trace entries between journal and ledger; computer systems link them automatically.

options: The side with the smaller total
The side with the larger total
mcqs.explain: Balance c/d (carried down) is the figure written on the side with the smaller total, so that both sides add up to the same amount. It is then brought down on the opposite side as Balance b/d to start the next period. The tempting option, 'the side with the larger total', reverses the rule — adding to the heavier side would never equalise the totals. In practice: every ledger account balanced at 31 March shows Balance c/d on the lighter side.

mcqs.q: A creditor had an opening balance of ₹20,000. Goods bought on credit ₹45,000; cash paid ₹38,000; goods returned ₹2,000. The closing balance is:
mcqs.explain: A creditor's account increases on the credit side. Credits: opening balance ₹20,000 + credit purchases ₹45,000 = ₹65,000. Debits: cash paid ₹38,000 + goods returned ₹2,000 = ₹40,000. Balance = ₹65,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹25,000 Cr, still owed to the creditor. The tempting ₹29,000 Cr adds the returns instead of deducting them. In practice: suppliers send a statement of account each quarter, and the buyer's accountant matches it with this closing balance.

mcqs.q: Salary ₹10,000 and wages ₹6,000 are paid by one cheque. In the Bank Account, the credit side shows:
options: By Salary A/c ₹10,000 and By Wages A/c ₹6,000
mcqs.explain: The entry is Salary A/c Dr. ₹10,000, Wages A/c Dr. ₹6,000, To Bank A/c ₹16,000. In the Bank Account, the credit side names each account debited with its own amount: 'By Salary A/c ₹10,000' and 'By Wages A/c ₹6,000'. The tempting option, 'To Salary A/c ₹16,000', uses 'To' (which belongs on the debit side) and lumps both amounts under salary. In practice: bank ledgers in accounting software show such payments split by expense head.

model.text: Anita's account closes without a balance. Sales is a nominal account: it is balanced here only for an interim (month-end) trial balance, so its balance is brought down on 1 September; at the year end it is not carried forward but closed by transfer to the Trading Account.

scheme.pt: Cash account: receipts To Capital, To Anita, To Sales; payments By Purchases, By Rent
Cash balance c/d ₹1,99,000 and b/d on 1 September
Sales account: By Anita, By Cash; balance ₹58,000
Anita account: To Sales; By Cash ₹35,000 and By Discount Allowed ₹1,000 — closed

remarks: Many candidates write "To" on the credit side or "By" on the debit side — this costs presentation marks in every account.
Anita's account is often left with a balance because the discount of ₹1,000 is forgotten.
mistakes: Posting the discount into Cash account.
Not bringing the balance down (b/d) on 1 September.
Balancing a closed account with a zero "balance c/d".
tips: Write the account name in the centre with Dr. and Cr. at the two corners.
Rule off totals on the same line on both sides.

questions.q: What is meant by balancing an account? Describe the steps, and state which accounts are not carried forward at the end of the year.

model.text: Balancing means finding the difference between the two sides of an account at the end of a period and recording it so that the account shows its net position.

items: Total both sides of the account.
Write the difference on the side with the smaller total as "Balance c/d", so both totals are equal.
Rule off and write the equal totals on the same line.
Bring the balance down on the opposite side as "Balance b/d" on the first day of the next period.

model.text: Nominal accounts (expenses, losses, incomes, gains) are not carried forward: they are closed by transfer to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account. Personal and real accounts are carried forward.

scheme.pt: Steps: totalling, balance c/d on lighter side, ruling off
Balance b/d on opposite side next period
Nominal accounts closed to Trading/P&L, not carried forward

remarks: Answers that list the steps in order score well.
Many forget the second part of the question about nominal accounts.
mistakes: Saying the balance c/d goes on the heavier side.
Saying all accounts are carried forward.
tips: Answer every part of the question — look for the word "and".

questions.q: On 9 September 2026 a business paid salaries ₹24,000, wages ₹16,000 and the electricity bill ₹5,000 by a single cheque. Show the journal entry and post it to the ledger (no balancing needed).

entries.narr: Being salaries, wages and the electricity bill paid by one cheque

scheme.pt: Compound journal entry with total ₹45,000 and narration
Bank account credited with three separate "By" lines (or By Sundries ₹45,000)
Each expense account debited "To Bank A/c" with its own amount

remarks: Some candidates debit Bank — read whether money comes in or goes out.
mistakes: Writing "To Sundries" in the expense accounts.
Posting the total ₹45,000 to every expense account.
tips: In a compound entry the single account lists the others; the others each name the single account.

summary: The ledger groups journal entries account by account.
Debited account: debit side, "To" + other account. Credited account: credit side, "By" + other account.
Balance c/d on the lighter side; balance b/d on the opposite side next period.
Personal and real accounts are carried forward; nominal accounts are closed to Trading/P&L.
remember: "To" always on the debit side, "By" always on the credit side.
J.F. in the ledger, L.F. in the journal.
traps: Don't write the balance c/d on the heavier side.
Don't post a compound entry's total to each account.

quickref.v: Debit side of that account: "To <account credited>"
Credit side of that account: "By <account debited>"
Difference on the lighter side as Balance c/d; Balance b/d on the opposite side next period

viva.q: What is a ledger, and why is it called the principal book of account?
viva.model: A ledger is a book that groups all transactions account by account, so each account shows its complete history in one place, while the journal keeps them in date order. It is called the principal book because the trial balance and the final accounts are prepared from the ledger balances.

cases.title: Sunil's account in the books of Ojas Traders
cases.case: On 1 April 2026 Sunil owed Ojas Traders ₹12,000. During April, Ojas Traders sold goods to Sunil on credit for ₹30,000, received ₹25,000 from him in cash, accepted goods worth ₹2,000 returned by him, and allowed him a cash discount of ₹500. Sunil's account is balanced on 30 April.

mcqs.q: On which side of Sunil's account is the cash of ₹25,000 posted, and how?
mcqs.explain: Sunil gives the cash, so under the personal account rule his account is credited. Credit-side postings start with 'By' followed by the name of the other account in the entry, so the posting reads 'By Cash ₹25,000'. The tempting option, 'Credit side — To Cash', has the correct side but the wrong prefix; 'To' is used only on the debit side. In practice: a customer's ledger shows each receipt as a credit with the cash or bank account named.

mcqs.q: What is the balance of Sunil's account on 30 April?
mcqs.explain: Debit side: opening balance ₹12,000 + credit sales ₹30,000 = ₹42,000. Credit side: cash ₹25,000 + returns ₹2,000 + discount ₹500 = ₹27,500. Balance = ₹42,000 − ₹27,500 = ₹14,500 Dr, meaning Sunil still owes the business. The tempting ₹15,000 Dr forgets the ₹500 discount allowed, which also reduces what Sunil owes. In practice: this closing balance is what Ojas Traders would show as Sunil's outstanding amount in its receivables ageing report.

mcqs.q: Where is "Balance c/d" written when the account is closed on 30 April?
options: It is not written; only b/d is shown
mcqs.explain: Balance c/d is written on the lighter side to make both totals equal. Here the credit side (₹27,500) is lighter than the debit side (₹42,000), so 'By Balance c/d ₹14,500' goes on the credit side. The tempting option, the debit side, is where the balance will be brought down next month, not where it is carried down. In practice: when accounts are closed monthly, every customer account with a debit balance shows Balance c/d on its credit side.

mcqs.q: What will be the first entry in the account on 1 May?
options: To Balance b/d ₹14,500 on the debit side
By Balance b/d ₹14,500 on the credit side
To Sales ₹30,000 on the debit side
By Cash ₹25,000 on the credit side
mcqs.explain: The balance carried down on the credit side on 30 April is brought down on the opposite side on 1 May: 'To Balance b/d ₹14,500' on the debit side, showing that Sunil owes this amount at the start of the new period. The tempting option, 'By Balance b/d on the credit side', would turn Sunil into a creditor. In practice: opening balances in accounting software carry forward automatically on the same side as the closing balance.
